input: Learn to read an architectural floor plan

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Floor plans range from basic residential layouts to complex commercial or structural drawings — knowing the type determines which symbols, scales, and conventions to focus on.
Whether this is for personal use (e.g. renovating a home), professional development, or academic study completely changes the depth and direction of learning needed.
If the user already has a specific floor plan in hand to work with, the plan can be hands-on and practical; if not, finding suitable example plans becomes a first step.
The available time window (a weekend crash course vs. a few months) shapes how much content to cover and at what pace.
Some people learn best through videos, others through books, guided courses, or hands-on practice — the preferred learning style determines which resources to recommend.

Success could mean understanding room dimensions and flow, identifying structural elements, interpreting electrical/plumbing symbols, or being able to spot errors — the target level defines when the task is done.
Knowing whether the user wants a self-guided resource list, a structured study schedule, or a step-by-step walkthrough determines the format of the plan output.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to read an architectural floor plan
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to develop the ability to read and interpret architectural floor plans from scratch or improve their existing understanding.

questions.title: What type of floor plan do you need to read?
questions.description: Is this a residential home, apartment, commercial building, or another type? The conventions and symbols differ significantly across plan types.

questions.title: Why do you need to read floor plans?
questions.description: For example: renovating your own home, a new job role, a school or university course, or general curiosity? The purpose shapes the required depth.

questions.title: Do you already have a specific floor plan to work from?
questions.description: Having a real plan in hand enables a practical, example-driven approach; without one, sourcing suitable sample plans becomes an early step.

questions.title: How much time can you dedicate to this learning goal?
questions.description: A single weekend, a few hours per week over a month, or an open-ended timeline all require very different pacing and depth of coverage.

questions.title: How do you learn best — videos, books, or hands-on practice?
questions.description: Preferred learning format determines which resources (YouTube tutorials, reference books, tracing exercises, etc.) to prioritise in the plan.

questions.title: What does successfully reading a floor plan look like for you?
questions.description: For instance: understanding room sizes and flow, reading structural or MEP symbols, spotting design issues, or confidently discussing plans with architects or contractors.

questions.title: What format should your learning plan take?
questions.description: Do you want a curated resource list, a day-by-day study schedule, a step-by-step skill walkthrough, or something else as your output?
